package_info.package_versions: 2.3.5 - 2.3.31, 2.5 - 2.5.10 (inclusive of all known-vulnerable versions, e.g., struts2-core-2.3.5.jar, struts2-core-2.5.10.jar)
package_info.why_malicious: The package itself is not intentionally malicious, but specific versions contain a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2017-5638) due to improper handling of user-supplied input in the Jakarta Multipart parser. Exploitation allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server by sending crafted HTTP requests, leading to full system compromise if unpatched versions are used.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the application processes an HTTP request containing a crafted Content-Type header (typically during file upload handling).
required_permissions: filesystem (for file upload handling and potential payload writing)
process execution (to execute arbitrary commands via OGNL injection)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
String contentType = request.getHeader("Content-Type");
Object value = ognlUtil.getValue(contentType, context, root);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: The code retrieves the Content-Type header from the incoming HTTP request and evaluates its value as an OGNL (Object-Graph Navigation Language) expression without sanitization. This allows an attacker to inject malicious OGNL expressions in the Content-Type header, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Evaluating untrusted user input (HTTP headers) as code is a severe security flaw. This enables attackers to inject OGNL expressions that the server will execute, leading to remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Web frameworks should never evaluate HTTP headers or any user-supplied input as executable code. Proper implementations strictly separate data from code and validate or sanitize all inputs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: OGNL evaluation is legitimate when parsing internal, trusted configuration or template expressions, but never on direct user input such as HTTP headers.
key_indicators: Direct use of user-supplied HTTP header (Content-Type) in OGNL expression evaluation
Absence of input validation or sanitization before code execution
OGNL evaluation invoked during HTTP request processing
Code path present in JakartaMultiPartRequest class in vulnerable Struts versions

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends an HTTP request with a specially crafted Content-Type header containing a malicious OGNL expression to the vulnerable Struts application (typically targeting file upload endpoints).
attack_chain.leads_to: The OGNL expression in the Content-Type header is evaluated by the vulnerable code in JakartaMultiPartRequest.

attack_chain.action: The injected OGNL expression is executed on the server, allowing the attacker to run arbitrary system commands (such as spawning a shell, downloading and executing malware, or exfiltrating sensitive data).
attack_chain.leads_to: Full compromise of the application server, including potential lateral movement or data breach.

behavioral_signatures: OGNL expression evaluation triggered by HTTP request headers (especially Content-Type) during request processing
Unexpected execution of system commands (e.g., /bin/sh, cmd.exe) by the Java application server process
Abnormal process creation or child processes spawned by the Java process in response to HTTP requests
Unusual error messages or stack traces referencing OGNL or JakartaMultiPartRequest in server logs
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable Struts JARs (e.g., struts2-core-2.3.5.jar, struts2-core-2.3.31.jar, struts2-core-2.5.10.jar) in application dependencies
Unexpected changes or additions to web.xml or Struts configuration files that enable multipart parsing
Artifacts of exploitation such as dropped web shells or suspicious files in upload directories
network_indicators: Inbound HTTP requests with Content-Type headers containing OGNL syntax (e.g., #cmd=, java.lang.Runtime)
Outbound network connections from the application server to external or attacker-controlled hosts following suspicious HTTP requests
High volume of HTTP 500 errors or abnormal responses after receiving crafted requests
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor application dependencies for the presence of known-vulnerable Struts versions. Inspect HTTP request logs for Content-Type headers containing OGNL expressions or suspicious patterns. Correlate abnormal process creation or command execution events with incoming HTTP requests. Use file integrity monitoring to detect the presence of vulnerable Struts JARs and unexpected files in upload directories. Monitor for outbound connections from the application server following suspicious inbound requests.
